title: Speak sweetly
hookLine: speak insipid words and body and mind grow insipid (Asa di Var, ang 473)

cards: Taste a spoonful of dal before the salt goes in. It isn't bad, exactly. It isn't poisoned or burned.
It's just flat. Lifeless. You take one bite and push the bowl away.
Punjabi has a word for that taste: fikka. Tea without sugar is fikka. A party where nobody talks is fikka.
And Guru Nanak used the same kitchen word, in a salok of the Asa di Var, for a kind of speech. Not lying, which we met two days ago. Something more ordinary, and maybe more common.

teach.b: The salok is on ang 473. In paraphrase: speaking fikka words, the body and mind become fikka.

teach.h: FIKKA WORDS MAKE A FIKKA PERSON.
teach.b: The fikka person is called fikka; the fikka person gets a fikka name. The fikka are cast out of the Court of the Lord, and have their faces spat upon. The fikka are called fools, and are punished with shoes.
The word repeats until you can taste it. Fikka here means insipid, but it leans toward harsh, rude, sour: words with no sweetness and no care in them. A curt reply.
A sarcastic dig. A cold one-word answer to someone who needed more. Here's the turn.
The salok doesn't only say fikka words hurt the listener. It says they make the speaker fikka, body and mind. Speak flat and sour long enough, and you become flat and sour.
Your reputation follows: people start to call you that. Anyone who's watched a person harden over the years has seen it happen. Words aren't just output.
Every sentence trains the one who says it. This connects back to mitthat neevee from day five hundred fifty-one: sweetness and humility as the essence of virtue. That was about who you are.
Today is about how you get there. Sweet speech isn't flattery or fake niceness.
It means words with some care cooked into them.
Salt in the dal. Sugar in the tea. Something that makes the other person want to stay at the table.

how: Sikhs hear this salok on fikka speech in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and sweet, humble speech is counted among the marks of a Sikh's character.

o: speech that hides the hard truth
speech with care cooked into it
flattery that makes others like you

games.q: fikka and sweet — tap the pairs.

s: the salok says harsh words only hurt the listener
it says they make the speaker's body and mind fikka too.
fikka is an everyday Punjabi word for flat, tasteless food
tea without sugar, dal without salt.
sweet speech in Sikh teaching means flattery
it means true words with care in them, not fake niceness.

games.q: you're tired, and someone asks you a question for the third time. you're about to snap. what does the salok say snapping does?
o: it makes you fikka, body and mind.
games.why: speaking fikka words, body and mind become fikka. every sentence trains the one who says it.

practice: Think of the last flat or sharp thing you said to someone, and without scolding yourself, just hear it again. Now imagine it with care cooked in: the same truth, a warmer sentence. If you pray, say Waheguru first.

wordCard.voice: Speak sweetly. Guru Nanak's warning about fikka words, flat and harsh like dal without salt: they make the body and mind of the speaker fikka too.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: fikka, insipid, tasteless, harsh; an everyday kitchen word Guru Nanak uses for speech.

carryVoice: Your line: sweet words, sweet life. Every sentence trains the one who says it. See you tomorrow.
